Learning Objectives
Review the epidemiology and etiology of various chondrogenic lesions of bone.
Discuss appropriate workup and diagnosis of chondrogenic lesions of bone.
Compare and contrast the clinical, radiographic, and histologic differences between common
chondrogenic lesions of bone.
Review hereditary cancer syndromes associated with chondrogenic lesions of bone.
Review general treatment principles for common benign and malignant chondrogenic lesions
of bone.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview

Chondrogenic lesions are found in patients of almost all ages and can arise in any location in a
bone.
The skeletal location of chondrogenic lesions is important.
Surgical management of chondrogenic lesions depends on the location and grade of the
tumor.
In general, malignant chondrogenic lesions of bone do not respond well to chemotherapy and
radiation therapy.

Overview
Chondrogenic lesions located in the axial skeleton are more suspicious for malignancy,
whereas lesions in the appendicular skeleton, especially the bones of the hands and
feet, are more likely to be benign. Wide resection and reconstruction are the surgical
goals for high-grade malignant chondrogenic lesions. Simple excision or intralesional
surgical management via local adjuvant treatment options are performed for benign
chondrogenic lesions.
Epidemiology
Patients younger than 40 years with a chondrogenic lesion of bone likely have a benign lesion
(Table 1).
Osteochondroma is the most common benign bone lesion.
Enchondroma is the most common bone tumor in the hand.
The incidence of secondary chondrosarcoma varies based on underlying risk factors/cause.

Epidemiology
The patient age range for and incidence of enchondroma and osteochondroma are wide
because many patients are asymptomatic and the lesions go undetected for extended
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:40 AM
AAOS | Chondrogenic Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000518
3/35

periods. Enchondromas are observed on approximately 2% of MRIs of the knee and
shoulder obtained for pain.1,2 Chondroblastomas are common in the epiphysis of
skeletally immature patients, with a substantial male predominance (approximate male-
to-female ratio of 2:1). The risk of malignant transformation ranges from less than 1% for
patients with a solitary osteochondroma, approximately 5% for patients with multiple
hereditary exostoses, 25% for patients with Ollier disease,3 to as high as 100% for
patients with Maffucci syndrome.3
Etiology
Benign Chondrogenic Lesions
Enchondroma
A benign cartilaginous lesion in the medullary cavity, most commonly in the metaphysis of a
long bone or in the bones of the hands and feet
Etiology
Possibly results from incomplete endochondral ossification, with a part of the cartilaginous
epiphyseal plate persisting in the metaphysis
Mutations in IDH1 and IDH2 have been reported in patients with enchondroma and patients
with chondrosarcoma.4
Periosteal Chondroma
A benign cartilage tumor located on the surface of the bone and thought to arise from the
periosteum
No clear genetic etiology has been identified.
Osteochondroma
A benign osteocartilaginous extramedullary tumor
Etiology
Most likely arises from physeal cartilage in skeletally immature patients that protrudes
outward and grows through the cortex
Lesion must be contiguous with the medullary canal to be an osteochondroma
MHE is the associated genetic syndrome

9/3/26, 7:40 AM


Osteochondroma
MHE has an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance. The genes associated with the
condition are EXT1, EXT2, and EXT3. EXT1 and EXT2 are involved in heparan sulfate
synthesis.5 EXT1 mutations are associated with the most severe disease.6
Chondroblastoma
A rare, benign lesion classically located in the epiphysis of skeletally immature individuals
No clear genetic etiology has been identified.
Chondromyxoid Fibroma
A rare, benign lesion typically eccentrically located in the metaphysis of the long bones,
classically the proximal tibia
No clear genetic etiology has been identified
Malignant Chondrogenic Lesions
Chondrosarcoma
A malignant cartilaginous lesion most common in the axial skeleton of elderly patients
Mutations in IDH1 and IDH2 have been reported in patients with chondrosarcoma.4
Four histologic grades correlate with survival.
Grade 1: 60% of cases; best prognosis
Grade 2: 25% of cases
Grade 3: 5% of cases
Dedifferentiated: 10% of cases; poorest prognosis
Survival7: (Figure 1)

Mesenchymal Chondrosarcoma
An exceedingly rare, malignant cartilaginous lesion more common in the axial skeleton in
younger patients than classic chondrosarcoma.
Two primary translocations have been found.
t(8.8)(q13;q21): HEY1-NCOA28
t(13.21)(q10;q10)9
Secondary Chondrosarcoma
A malignant cartilaginous lesion arising from a previously benign lesion, such as an
enchondroma or osteochondroma.
Most commonly observed in patients with MHE, Ollier disease, or Maffucci syndrome.
Etiology typically is based on the underlying genetic mutations observed with the specific
syndrome.
Sporadic transformation of an isolated enchondroma or osteochondroma can occur but is rare
(<1%).

Clear Cell Chondrosarcoma
A rare, malignant cartilaginous lesion most common in the femoral head or epiphysis of other
long bones, with age at diagnosis similar to that for conventional chondrosarcoma.10
No clear genetic etiology or associated syndrome has been identified.
Workup/Diagnosis
Benign Chondrogenic Lesions
Enchondroma
Clinical presentation
Typically, enchondromas are painless and found incidentally on radiographs and other
imaging studies.
With enchondromas in the metaphysis adjacent to a joint, such as the shoulder or knee, any
pain experienced by the patient likely is from the adjacent joint rather than the
enchondroma.
Imaging workup/surveillance
If the enchondroma is visible on plain radiographs, interval follow-up with plain radiographs
is adequate.
Biopsy
Needle biopsy is not recommended to confirm the presence of an enchondroma with no
aggressive features on plain radiographs.
Management
Surgical management rarely is necessary; however intralesional curettage with bone grafting
or cementing and stabilization can be performed for recurrent fractures from an
enchondroma.

Enchondroma
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:40 AM
AAOS | Chondrogenic Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000518
7/35

An enchondroma of a bone in the axial skeleton, such as the scapula, the ilium, or a rib,
should be likely is a chondrosarcoma. Enchondromas may present as pain if associated
with pathologic fractures in the bones of the hand or feet and may have a more
aggressive radiographic appearance in these locations.
MRIs and CT scans are unnecessary for initial workup or surveillance of enchondromas
without aggressive features on plain radiographs.11 Bone scintigraphy is not useful for
initial workup or surveillance of enchondromas unless suspicion for Ollier disease or
Maffucci syndrome exists.11 Pain attributable to the lesion in combination with lesion
growth and/or cortical thinning, cortical breakthrough, or soft-tissue extension suggests
sarcomatous transformation.
Needle biopsy, even with experienced pathologists, may not reliably distinguish
enchondroma from low-grade chondrosarcoma, emphasizing the importance of changes
in symptoms and imaging findings to diagnose chondrosarcoma.12,13
Periosteal Chondroma
Clinical presentation
The lesions usually result in pain
May have slow growth, but malignant transformation is rare
Imaging workup/surveillance
Lucent surface lesion without intramedullary extent on plain radiographs
Biopsy
Needle biopsy may be useful to rule out other surface lesions
Management
Excision or intralesional curettage with burring, cementing, or bone grafting and adjuvant
treatment options are preferred.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:40 AM
AAOS | Chondrogenic Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000518
8/35


Periosteal Chondroma
MRIs and CT scans typically are unnecessary for initial workup unless more aggressive
etiologies, such as periosteal osteosarcoma, are included in the differential diagnosis.
Bone scintigraphy is not useful for initial workup or surveillance.
Osteochondroma
Clinical presentation
Most are asymptomatic in the metaphysis
Should not increase in size after skeletal maturity
Imaging workup/surveillance
Plain radiographs alone typically are adequate for diagnosis
Biopsy
Needle biopsy is not recommended to confirm the presence of an osteochondroma or to
confirm sarcomatous transformation of an existing osteochondroma
Management
Symptomatic lesions can be excised with reliable resolution of symptoms.
Asymptomatic, stable lesions can be observed.

Osteochondroma
Osteochondromas can cause pain from tendon snapping, bursa, or compression of
neurovascular structures depending on the size. If the size of the lesion increases after
skeletal maturity, sarcomatous transformation should be considered.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:40 AM

MRI is necessary only if new pain is present or growth of the cartilage cap or
neurovascular compression from the osteochondroma is suspected. Bone scintigraphy
or CT generally is not useful for initial workup or surveillance of isolated
osteochondromas. A cartilage cap greater than 2 cm or a growing cartilage cap is
concerning for malignant transformation in adults; however, cartilage cap thickness is
less relevant in children14 (Resource 1).
Chondroblastoma
Clinical presentation
Painful lucent lesion in the epiphysis of skeletally immature patients or young adults.
Imaging workup/surveillance
Plain radiographs are the first imaging study obtained and the mainstay of postoperative
imaging surveillance for local recurrence.
Biopsy
Needle biopsy typically is recommended to distinguish chondroblastoma from other
epiphyseal lesions, such as Brodie abscess, aneurysmal bone cysts, or giant cell tumors of
bone in young adults.
Management
Typically managed surgically via curettage, high-speed burring, cementing, or bone grafting
and, if necessary, internal fixation to prevent fracture.
Adjuvant treatment options, such as phenol and argon beam, also have been used.
Small lesions in challenging locations may be managed via radiofrequency ablation.

Chondroblastoma

MRI may be necessary for surgical planning and often exhibit perilesional edema. Bone
scintigraphy or CT generally is not useful for initial workup or surveillance.
Chondromyxoid Fibroma
Clinical presentation
Painful, lucent, eccentric lesion in the metaphysis of skeletally mature patients.
Most frequently in the proximal tibia
Imaging workup/surveillance
Plain radiographs are the first imaging study obtained and the mainstay of postoperative
imaging surveillance for local recurrence.
Biopsy
Needle biopsy typically is recommended to distinguish chondromyxoid fibroma from other
metaphyseal lesions in adults, including primary bone malignancies and chondromyxoid
fibroma–likeosteosarcoma.15
Management
Managed surgically via curettage, high-speed burring, cementing, or bone grafting and, if
necessary, internal fixation to prevent fracture.
Adjuvant treatment options, such as phenol and argon beam, also have been used.

Chondromyxoid Fibroma
MRI may be necessary for surgical planning. Bone scintigraphy or CT generally is not
useful for initial workup or surveillance.
Malignant Chondrogenic Lesions
SEND FEEDBACK

11/35

Chondrosarcoma
Clinical presentation
Pain in the area of a slow-growing mass in an older adult
More likely if the lesion is in the pelvis, proximal femur, scapula, ribs, or other bones of the
axial skeleton, including the spine
Less likely with painful lesions in the hands or feet
Imaging workup/surveillance
Plain radiographs typically demonstrate cortical erosion/endosteal scalloping, increased
cartilage matrix production, or cortical breakthrough, especially with grade 2, grade 3, or
dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma.
MRIs may show soft-tissue extension and occult lesion extension in the bone marrow that is
not readily visible on plain radiographs. MRIs also are obtained to help with surgical
planning.
Chest radiography or CT and whole-body bone scintigraphy are performed to complete
staging.
The lungs are the most common site for metastases, followed by another bone.
Biopsy
Routine needle biopsy of lesions suspicious for chondrosarcoma on imaging studies is
controversial because it may not reliably distinguish enchondroma from low-grade
chondrosarcoma in the extremities and cannot distinguish between chondrosarcoma grades
in the pelvis, emphasizing the importance of symptoms and imaging findings to diagnose
chondrosarcoma.12,13
If unclear whether an aggressive lesion in bone is of cartilaginous origin, needle biopsy is
recommended to exclude other diagnoses.
Management

9/3/26, 7:40 AM

12/35

Grade 1, appendicular skeleton: curettage, adjuvant treatment options, cementing, internal
fixation if necessary
Grade 1, axial skeleton: wide resection
Grade 2: wide resection
Grade 3: wide resection
Dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma: wide resection; chemotherapy also may be used, with the
regimen depending on the histology of the dedifferentiated tumor.
Systemic therapy generally is reserved for metastatic disease.
Adjuvant radiation therapy may be used in patients with positive surgical margins to
decrease the risk of local recurrence.16

Chondrosarcoma
Imaging of grade 1 chondrosarcoma may differ subtly from imaging of enchondroma
accompanied by pain. Local recurrence typically is monitored via a combination of plain
radiographs and MRIs or CT scans. Surveillance for pulmonary metastases is performed
via chest radiographs and/or chest CT scans.
Secondary Chondrosarcoma
Clinical presentation
Pain, lesion growth, and progressive imaging changes of a pre-existing enchondroma or
osteochondroma
More common in patients with known MHE, Ollier disease, or Maffucci syndrome
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:40 AM
AAOS | Chondrogenic Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000518
13/35

More likely if the lesion is in the pelvis, proximal femur, scapula, ribs, or other bones of the
axial skeleton, including the spine
Prognosis is based on the size and grade of the lesion, which is the same as that for primary
chondrosarcoma.
Imaging workup/surveillance
Plain radiographs typically demonstrate aggressive features, such as cortical
erosion/endosteal scalloping, increased cartilage matrix production, or cortical
breakthrough, especially with grade 2, grade 3, or dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma.
MRIs may show soft-tissue extension, a cartilage cap of more than 2 cm, and occult lesion
extension in the bone marrow not readily visible on plain radiographs. MRIs also are
obtained to aid in surgical planning.
Chest radiography or CT and whole-body bone scintigraphy are performed to complete
staging.
Biopsy
Routine needle biopsy of secondary chondrogenic lesions suspicious for sarcomatous
transformation on imaging studies generally is not necessary, especially in patients with a
known syndrome at risk for chondrosarcoma.
If unclear whether an aggressive lesion in bone is of cartilaginous origin, needle biopsy is
recommended to exclude other diagnoses.
Management
Grade 1, appendicular skeleton: curettage, adjuvant treatment options, cementing, internal
fixation if necessary
Grade 1, axial skeleton: wide resection
Grade 2: wide resection
Grade 3: wide resection

Dedifferentiated chondrosarcoma: wide resection; chemotherapy also may be used, with the
regimen depending on the histology of the dedifferentiated tumor.
Systemic therapy generally is reserved for metastatic disease.
Adjuvant radiation therapy may be used for positive surgical margins to decrease the risk of
local recurrence.16

Secondary Chondrosarcoma
Local recurrence typically is monitored via a combination of plain radiographs and MRIs
or CT scans. Surveillance for pulmonary metastases is performed via chest radiographs
and/or chest CT scans.
Clear Cell Chondrosarcoma
Clinical presentation
Pain and a lesion in the epiphysis in the long bone of an older adult
Most common in the femoral head
Other areas, such as the pelvis, scapula, ribs, or other bones of the axial skeleton, including
the spine, may be involved.
Imaging workup/surveillance
Plain radiographs typically demonstrate a lytic lesion in the epiphysis that may be confused
with chondroblastoma; however, the patient should be much older than a patient with the
typical presentation of chondroblastoma.
MRIs may show soft-tissue extension and occult lesion extension in the bone marrow not
readily visible on plain radiographs. MRIs also are obtained to aid in surgical planning.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:40 AM
AAOS | Chondrogenic Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000518
15/35

Chest radiography or CT and whole-body bone scintigraphy are performed to complete
staging.
Biopsy
Routine needle biopsy is recommended because a lucent epiphyseal lesion in older adults
may be the result of metastatic disease, infection, or giant cell tumor of bone, among other
etiologies.
Management
Wide resection
Systemic therapy generally is reserved for metastatic disease.

Clear Cell Chondrosarcoma
Local recurrence typically is monitored via a combination of plain radiographs and MRIs
or CT scans. Surveillance for pulmonary metastases is performed via chest radiographs
and/or chest CT scans.
Mesenchymal Chondrosarcoma
Clinical presentation
Pain in the area of a slow-growing mass in an adult who is younger than an adult with
conventional chondrosarcoma
More common in the flat bones of the axial skeleton
Imaging workup/surveillance
Plain radiographs typically demonstrate lytic destruction of the bone with cartilage matrix.
MRIs may show soft-tissue extension and occult lesion extension in the bone marrow not
readily visible on plain radiographs. MRIs also are obtained to aid surgical planning.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:40 AM
AAOS | Chondrogenic Lesions
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000518
16/35

Chest radiography or CT and whole-body bone scintigraphy are performed to complete
staging.
Biopsy
Routine needle biopsy generally is recommended because the radiographic appearance
often is not diagnostic of a cartilage lesion.
Mesenchymal chondrosarcoma is the only chondrosarcoma subtype that has an acceptable
response to chemotherapeutic agents; therefore, needle biopsy may allow for neoadjuvant
systemic management.14
Management
Wide resection
In general, chemotherapy also is used because these tumors are associated with a high rate
of metastatic disease, an aggressive clinical course, and poor prognosis.

Mesenchymal Chondrosarcoma
Local recurrence typically is monitored via a combination of plain radiographs and MRIs
or CT scans. Surveillance for pulmonary metastases is performed via chest radiographs
and/or chest CT scans.

bone scan shows shortening of the right lower limb, varus deformity of the femur, and valgus

femur and tibia. AP radiographs of the right knee (B) and lower leg (C) demonstrate deformity of
the distal femur and the tibia and fibula. Structural changes observed in the marrow cavity and
the cortical bone of the femur and tibia consist of osteolysis and osteosclerosis. Areas of
mineralization (calcifications; arrow) are observed in the proximal tibia. The appearance is
consistent with multiple chondromatous tumors. D, Coronal, fat-suppressed, contrast-enhanced
T1-weighted MRI of the femur shows varus deformity. Multiple, partially lobulated areas with
increased signal intensity are observed because of the chondromatous lesions. A large lesion is
observed in the distal femur (arrow). The enhancement demonstrates rings and arcs (also known
as septal or nodular enhancement) consistent with the chondromatous nature of the lesions
